critical_path.title: Happy Path: Successful User Login with Standard Credentials
critical_path.description: Verifies a registered user can successfully authenticate using their username and password. This is the most critical end-to-end user journey and establishes a baseline for performance, visual integrity, and accessibility of the post-login experience. Gherkin: Given I am a registered user on the login page, When I enter my valid username and password and click 'Sign in', Then I should be redirected to my dashboard and see my profile information.
prerequisites: A valid, active test account (e.g., 'qa-bot-2025') must exist in the system.
The test environment is stable and all dependent services are running.

steps.expected: The GitHub login form is fully loaded and interactive within 3 seconds (FCP < 1.5s).

selector.description: Selector for the username/email input field.

steps.expected: The text 'qa-bot-2025' is entered into the username field.

selector.description: Selector for the password input field.

steps.expected: The password is entered into the password field (masked).

selector.description: Selector for the primary 'Sign in' submit button.

steps.expected: A POST request to the authentication endpoint is triggered.

assertions: Mutation-Resistant Assertion: The URL of the page must be 'https://github.com/' and an element with the selector for the user's profile avatar (e.g., 'img.avatar.avatar-user') must be visible.
Performance Budget: The server response time for the login POST request must be < 400ms. The post-login dashboard page must have a Time To Interactive (TTI) of < 2 seconds.
Visual AI Checkpoint: A screenshot of the user dashboard is captured and compared against the approved baseline. The perceptual difference must be less than 2%.
Accessibility Assertion: Run an automated accessibility scan (e.g., axe-core) on the post-login dashboard. The scan must report zero 'critical' or 'serious' WCAG 2.2 Level AA violations.
cleanup: Perform a full logout action to terminate the session.
Clear all session cookies for the 'github.com' domain.

critical_path.title: Integration & Alternate Path: Successful Login via Google SSO
critical_path.description: Validates the end-to-end user journey for authentication via the 'Continue with Google' single sign-on (SSO) provider. This test focuses on the integration contract and performance of the redirect flow. Gherkin: Given I am a user with a GitHub account linked to Google, When I click 'Continue with Google', Then I should complete the Google auth flow and be logged into my GitHub dashboard.
prerequisites: A test GitHub account exists and is linked to a test Google account.
A consumer-driven contract test (e.g., Pact) has been run and passed, verifying GitHub's expectations of the Google OAuth API response schema.

steps.action: Pre-flight Check: Run Consumer Contract Test
steps.expected: The contract verification passes, confirming the expected API interaction is still valid.
The login form is displayed.

selector.description: Selector for the Google SSO button.

steps.expected: The user is redirected to the Google authentication portal.

steps.data: Simulated or real interaction with Google's login and consent screen.
steps.expected: User is authenticated with Google and redirected back to GitHub.

assertions: Integration Assertion: During the flow, the browser URL must at some point contain 'accounts.google.com'.
Successful Login Assertion: After the redirect back from Google, the final URL must be 'https://github.com/' and the user's profile avatar must be visible.
Performance Budget: The initial redirect from GitHub to Google must occur in < 500ms. The total time from clicking the SSO button to the GitHub dashboard being interactive must be < 4 seconds.

Metamorphic Testing Property: If the user is already logged into Google, the authentication flow should require fewer steps (e.g., no password entry) than if they are not logged in. This invariant property should always hold true.
cleanup: Perform a full logout from GitHub.
Navigate to Google and perform a logout to clear the SSO session.
Clear all session cookies for both 'github.com' and 'google.com' domains.

critical_path.description: Validates the primary user authentication journey with a valid username and password. This is the most critical happy path. This test incorporates 2025 best practices by embedding performance budgets, visual regression checkpoints, and accessibility scans into the core functional flow. It ensures the login is not just successful, but also fast, visually correct, and usable by everyone.
prerequisites: A valid, active GitHub test account must exist.
The test environment must be stable and networked.
Visual AI baseline image for the post-login dashboard must be captured.

steps.expected: The page loads successfully. The 'Sign in to GitHub' title is visible.

steps.action: WHEN I type my username into the login field
steps.expected: The username is correctly entered in the input field.

steps.action: AND I type my password into the password field
steps.expected: The password is masked and entered correctly.

steps.action: AND I click the 'Sign in' button
steps.expected: The form is submitted, and a navigation to the user dashboard is initiated.

steps.action: THEN I should be redirected to my dashboard
steps.expected: The URL should be 'https://github.com/' and the page title should reflect the user's dashboard. A user profile avatar should be visible in the header.

assertions: Assert the final URL is 'https://github.com/' and does NOT contain '/login'.
Assert the page title is 'GitHub'.
Assert the presence of the user's avatar/profile dropdown in the top-right header.
Performance Budget: Assert that the time from clicking 'Sign in' to the dashboard's `domContentLoaded` event is less than 1500ms.
Visual AI Checkpoint: Assert the post-login dashboard matches the baseline with a 99.5% similarity threshold, ignoring dynamic content regions.
Accessibility Check: Assert the login form and post-login page have zero critical violations when scanned against WCAG 2.2 Level AA rules.
cleanup: Perform a logout action to invalidate the session.
Clear browser cookies and session storage.

validation.title: TC1: Required Field Validation and Server-Side Enforcement
validation.description: This critical test verifies that submitting an empty form triggers client-side validation with clear, user-friendly error messages. It also ensures that the backend performs its own validation, preventing form submission even if client-side checks are bypassed. This confirms a fundamental security and usability principle.

risk_assessment.impact: High (Users cannot log in, potential for server errors if validation is client-side only)
risk_assessment.likelihood: Medium (Common user action, potential for malicious probing)
risk_assessment.mitigation: Enforce mandatory server-side validation and provide clear client-side feedback.

prerequisites: Navigate to https://github.com/login
Ensure no active session exists by clearing cookies and local storage.

steps.expected: The 'Username or email address' and 'Password' fields are visible and empty.
A validation error message is displayed on the page without a full page reload.

functional: Assert that an error message container is visible.
Assert that the error message text is exactly 'Incorrect username or password.' (This is GitHub's actual message for empty/wrong credentials, testing the real system behavior).
Assert that the URL remains 'https://github.com/session' (the POST endpoint) or redirects back to '/login', but does not proceed to the user dashboard.

api_contract_test.expectation: The server must respond with a 4xx status code (e.g., 422 Unprocessable Entity), not a 5xx server error. The response body should not leak any internal system details.

performance_budget.notes: Validation responses must be extremely fast to provide immediate feedback.

assertions_and_checks.accessibility_check: Verify the error message container has a `role='alert'` and is programmatically linked to the input fields via `aria-describedby` for screen reader users (WCAG 2.2).
assertions_and_checks.visual_regression_checkpoint: Capture a screenshot of the form with the error message and compare it against the approved 'Login Error' baseline in the visual testing tool.
assertions_and_checks.mutation_testing_resistance: The assertion on the exact error text ensures that a mutation changing the validation logic (e.g., allowing empty strings) would cause this test to fail.

validation.flakiness_mitigation: Use explicit waits for the error message to appear after the click, with a timeout of 3 seconds. Disable animations during the test run to ensure consistent rendering.
validation.test_impact_analysis: This test is highly stable as it relies on core form elements. It will only fail if the form structure, field IDs, or the fundamental server validation logic is changed.

error_handling.title: Chaos Test: System handles 503 Service Unavailable error gracefully during login attempt
error_handling.description: This chaos engineering test simulates a critical backend failure. It intercepts the login network request and forces a 503 'Service Unavailable' response. The test validates that the frontend does not crash, displays a user-friendly error message, preserves non-sensitive user input (username), and logs the event for observability.
prerequisites: Test automation framework must have network interception capabilities (e.g., Playwright's page.route, Cypress's cy.intercept).
Network intercept is configured to catch POST requests to 'https://github.com/session' and respond with a 503 status.

    When I click the 'Sign in' button
    Then I should see a clear error message indicating a temporary server problem
    And the username 'test-user-dev' should still be present in the login field
    And the password field should be cleared for security
    And a client-side error should be logged with 'severity: error' and 'statusCode: 503'.

Assert that the value of the 'login_field' input is 'test-user-dev'.
Assert that the value of the 'password' input is an empty string.
Assert that the browser's console contains a log entry matching the expected error structure.

error_handling.title: Error Handling: User double-clicks submit button, ensuring idempotent UI response
error_handling.description: This test validates the system's resilience against accidental form resubmissions, a common user error. It ensures the 'Sign in' button is disabled immediately after the first click to prevent duplicate network requests, which could lead to race conditions or backend errors. This behavior is crucial for a stable and predictable user experience.
prerequisites: User is on the GitHub login page: https://github.com/login
Valid username and password have been entered into the form.

A short, explicit delay (e.g., 50ms) will be inserted between the two simulated clicks to mimic human speed and ensure the event listener registers both actions.
error_handling.test_impact_analysis: This test is tightly coupled to the submit button's state management logic. A failure indicates a potential regression in form submission handling or event listening. Maintenance is low as long as the form's core submission mechanism remains consistent. It protects against regressions in client-side validation frameworks.

Assert that the network call interceptor recorded exactly one POST request to the session creation endpoint.
Assert that no client-side error notifications are displayed.
error_handling.accessibility_checkpoint: Verify the submit button, when disabled, has `aria-disabled='true'` and is not focusable by keyboard navigation, ensuring WCAG 2.2 compliance.

error_handling.title: Edge Case: Race condition between standard login and 'Continue with Google' SSO
error_handling.description: This test identifies a potential race condition by initiating a standard login submission immediately followed by a click on the 'Continue with Google' SSO button. A robust system must gracefully handle this by canceling one flow and committing to the other, preventing a mixed state, multiple redirects, or application errors.
prerequisites: User is on the GitHub login page: https://github.com/login
Test environment has credentials for both standard and Google accounts.
error_handling.gherkin_scenario:
Feature: Concurrent Authentication Flow
  Scenario: User initiates two different login methods in rapid succession
    Given I have entered valid credentials in the login form
    When I click the 'Sign in' button
    And I immediately click the 'Continue with Google' button within 200ms
    Then the application should cancel the initial form submission request
    And should proceed exclusively with the Google authentication flow
    And the URL should change to reflect the Google OAuth endpoint
    And no 'invalid credentials' error from the first attempt should be displayed.

metamorphic_testing.property: The final authentication state should be deterministic, regardless of the order of closely-timed user inputs. The system must prioritize the last-initiated, user-driven authentication event.
metamorphic_testing.relation: Executing (Submit) then (SSO_Click) should result in the same final state as executing only (SSO_Click), effectively ignoring the first action.

error_handling.ai_expected_behavior: AI predicts that the initial POST request for the standard login will be initiated but then aborted by the browser as the page begins to navigate to the Google OAuth URL triggered by the second click. The final state will be a page redirect, not an in-page error.
error_handling.flakiness_mitigation: Test depends on precise timing. Use a programmatic approach to fire the two click events with a controlled, minimal delay (e.g., 50ms) rather than relying on test runner speed. The final assertion should be on the browser's URL location, which is a more stable indicator of outcome than transient UI elements.
error_handling.test_impact_analysis: A failure here points to a deep issue in the frontend's state management or routing logic. It is a high-value test for single-page applications with complex, competing user flows. It requires maintenance if the SSO implementation or providers change.
mutation_resistant_assertions: Assert that the browser's final URL contains 'accounts.google.com'.
Assert that the network inspector shows the POST request to '/session' was aborted or never completed.
Assert that no error message container is visible on the page before the redirect.

Clear all session and cookie data.

security.title: Security: Prevent SQL Injection (SQLi) Authentication Bypass in Username Field
security.description: Verifies that the login form is not vulnerable to a classic SQL injection attack intended to bypass authentication. This test submits a malicious string (`' OR 1=1 --`) in the username field, which would cause a naive SQL query to always return true, granting access. A secure system must sanitize this input and treat it as an invalid login attempt, returning a generic error message without exposing backend system details or performance degradation.
prerequisites: The test environment must be accessible.
The test automation framework must be configured to capture network responses (status codes and bodies).

steps.expected: The GitHub login page loads successfully, with username and password fields visible.

steps.action: Enter SQL injection payload into the username field
steps.expected: The malicious string is entered into the username field.
The password field is populated.
The form is submitted. The page displays a generic authentication error message. The user is NOT logged in and redirected to the dashboard.

assertions: The current URL must remain on or return to 'https://github.com/session'. It must NOT be a user dashboard URL.
An error message container must be visible with the text 'Incorrect username or password.'
The HTTP response for the form submission must be a client error (e.g., 401 Unauthorized or 422 Unprocessable Entity), not a success (200 OK followed by redirect) or server error (500).
The response body must NOT contain database error strings like 'SQL syntax error', 'ORA-', or 'Query failed'.
Performance Budget: The server response time for the login attempt must be under 800ms to ensure a heavy/malformed query is not causing database strain.
cleanup: Clear browser cookies and session storage to ensure a clean state for subsequent tests.

security.title: Security: Verify Brute Force Prevention via Account Lockout or Rate Limiting
security.description: This resilience test simulates a low-and-slow brute force attack to ensure the application implements protective measures like rate-limiting (e.g., HTTP 429 response) or temporary account lockout after a specific number of failed login attempts. This prevents attackers from using automated scripts to guess passwords. This test is crucial for protecting user accounts from credential stuffing attacks.
prerequisites: A valid, existing username for the test environment (e.g., 'test_user_for_lockout').
The test framework must be capable of making repeated API calls or UI interactions in a loop and inspecting HTTP response headers.

steps.action: Perform 5 consecutive failed login attempts for a valid user with an incorrect password.
steps.expected: For the first 4 attempts, the system should display the standard 'Incorrect username or password.' error. The server response time should be consistent and fast.

steps.action: On the 6th consecutive failed login attempt
steps.expected: The form is submitted. A different error message should appear, indicating that too many failed attempts have occurred. The user is prevented from attempting to log in again immediately.

assertions: After N (e.g., 5) failed attempts, the HTTP response status code for the POST to '/session' must be 429 (Too Many Requests).
The UI must display a message like 'You have performed too many attempts. Please wait a while before trying again.'
The 'Sign in' button may become disabled or a CAPTCHA challenge may appear.
Any subsequent login attempt within the lockout window (e.g., 1 minute) must also fail immediately with an HTTP 429 response, even with correct credentials, proving the rate limit is in effect.
Performance SLA: The rate-limiting response (HTTP 429) must be triggered within 100ms, indicating an efficient edge-level or middleware defense rather than a slow, application-level check.
cleanup: Wait for the lockout period to expire or use a privileged API to reset the lockout status for the test user to avoid impacting other tests.

security.title: Security - Prevent SQL Injection and DOM-Based XSS via Login Field
security.description: This test verifies that the application's input sanitization pipeline correctly neutralizes malicious payloads designed to execute arbitrary SQL commands and client-side scripts. It simulates a sophisticated attack attempting to bypass simple filters. Gherkin-style flow: Given a user is on the login page, When they enter a combined SQLi and XSS payload into the username field and submit, Then the submission must be rejected, no script should execute, and the application must return a generic error without revealing internal state.
prerequisites: The application is running at https://github.com/login.
The test runner has network throttling capabilities disabled for baseline measurement.

steps.expected: The input field should display the entered text. The application should not hang or crash.
The password field should mask the entered text.
The page should display a clear, generic error message indicating incorrect credentials. The URL should not change. No browser alert dialog should appear.

assertions: The server must respond with a non-5xx status code (e.g., 401 Unauthorized or 422 Unprocessable Entity).
The browser's alert dialog count must be 0.
The DOM must not contain a new '<svg>' element.

  This test simulates a scenario where the third-party Google Sign-In script is blocked (e.g., by a corporate firewall, browser extension, or regional outage). It verifies that the application handles this failure gracefully by informing the user and ensuring the primary username/password login functionality remains unaffected.

  @high
  @general
  Scenario: Graceful Degradation when Third-Party SSO Script Fails to Load
    Background:
      * A chaos tool or browser setting must be configured to block any network requests to domains like 'apis.google.com' or 'accounts.google.com'.
    Given CHAOS: Activate network block for Google domains
    Then The chaos condition is now active.
    Given I Navigate to URL "https://github.com/login" in "None"
    Then The GitHub login page loads completely, even though the Google script failed in the background. No console errors crash the main application thread.
    When click
    Then An inline, user-friendly error message appears near the 'Continue with Google' button (e.g., 'Google sign-in is currently unavailable. Please use your password.'). The page does not crash or freeze.
    Then Verify interactability
    Then Verify interactability
    Then The primary login form (`#login_field`, `#password`) must remain enabled and interactive after the SSO button click fails.
    Then A specific, visible error message related to the SSO failure must be present in the DOM.
    Then Mutation-Resistant Assertion: Assert that `window.google` or the relevant SDK object is `undefined` to confirm the chaos injection worked.
    Then Accessibility: The error message must be linked to the button via `aria-describedby` for screen reader users.
    Then Contract Test (Implicit): The UI's resilience demonstrates it does not have a hard contract with the Google SDK; it anticipates its potential absence.

chaos_engineering.title: Resilience against Corrupted Client-Side Storage on Page Load
chaos_engineering.description: This test simulates a user returning to the login page with corrupted data in their `localStorage`. A resilient application should defensively handle this by catching parsing errors and loading the page in a clean state, rather than crashing. This validates the robustness of the application's initialization logic.
prerequisites: The test runner must have the ability to execute JavaScript in the browser context to manipulate `localStorage` before the page's main scripts run.

steps.action: Navigate to a blank page on the same domain
steps.expected: Browser is on the correct origin to set localStorage.

steps.action: CHAOS: Inject corrupted data into localStorage
steps.expected: Malformed data is now present in `localStorage`.

alternative_selectors.ai_hint: Element that CHAOS: Inject corrupted data into localStorage with Malformed data is now present in `localStorage`.

steps.expected: The GitHub login page loads completely without any visible errors or crashes. The UI is fully rendered and interactive.
The browser's developer console does not contain any uncaught 'SyntaxError: JSON.parse' or 'TypeError' exceptions that would halt script execution.

alternative_selectors.ai_hint: Element that Check for console errors with The browser's developer console does not contain any uncaught 'SyntaxError: JSON.parse' or 'TypeError' exceptions that would halt script execution.

steps.expected: The username field accepts text input correctly, proving the UI is not frozen.

alternative_selectors.ai_hint: Element that type_text with The username field accepts text input correctly, proving the UI is not frozen.

assertions: The `<body>` element is present and visible.
The login form input `#login_field` is visible and enabled.

Property-Based Test Invariant: The login page's core interactive elements (`#login_field`, `#password`, submit button) must always be rendered and enabled on page load, regardless of the state of `localStorage`.

Test Oracle Generation: An AI model predicts that given corrupted `localStorage`, the expected behavior is a default, clean login form, not a blank page or error screen. The test validates this prediction.
Flakiness Mitigation: This test is highly stable as it controls the client state directly before navigation, avoiding timing issues.
cleanup: Execute script to clear the specific `localStorage` key (`localStorage.removeItem('github:user-session')`).
